clue.text: Station alteration - good to be replaced with new line

indicators.note: one letter is swapped out of the word and another put in its place

blocks.note: an alteration is a change
G is the usual abbreviation for good
N is the abbreviation for new
L is the abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: A broadcaster's schedule shake-up: the good programme gets dropped for a new line-up.
explanation.walkthrough: In CHANGE the G gives way to N, making CHANNE, and L is then added on the end to make CHANNEL.
explanation.definitionFit: A television or radio station is commonly called a channel, the frequency band it broadcasts on.

clue.text: The best stuff to conserve energy

indicators.note: to conserve something is to keep it safe inside, so one piece is held within the other

blocks.note: to stuff is to cram
E is the symbol for energy

explanation.surface: Advice on the best stuff for saving energy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stuff' looks like a noun after 'best'; it is the verb, to pack tightly.
explanation.definitionFit: The cream is the finest part of anything, from the richest part of milk rising to the top.

clue.text: Strauss heroine's operatic song upset finale

indicators.note: upset means turned over, so in a down clue the word is read upwards

blocks.note: an aria is a solo song in an opera
a finale is the end

explanation.surface: The heroine of a Strauss opera's big song wrecking the finale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Operatic song' and 'Strauss heroine' both sound musical, so the definition hides in plain sight at the start.
explanation.definitionFit: Ariadne is the title heroine of Richard Strauss's opera Ariadne auf Naxos, from the Greek myth.

clue.text: Mutter, being made ill with inn food

indicators.note: something made ill is disordered, so these letters are thrown into disarray

blocks.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder
taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A grumble from someone made ill by pub food.
explanation.definitionFit: Nutriment is nourishment, anything eaten that sustains the body, so it means food.

clue.text: Proprietor putting limits to Liebfraumilch of greater vintage

blocks.note: the limits of the wine's name are its first and last letters, spelt out in words as L and H
something of greater vintage is older

explanation.surface: A wine merchant laying down an older vintage of Liebfraumilch, a German white wine.
explanation.walkthrough: The joining word in 'L and H' is kept as letters, an unusual trick: the end letters are read out as a phrase rather than just set side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: A landholder owns or holds land, making them its proprietor.

clue.text: Encouraging motor racing cartel

blocks.note: F1, Formula One, the top class of motor racing, with the numeral 1 read as the letter I
a ring is a group of traders fixing prices together

explanation.surface: A motor-racing cartel being encouraged, a sporting-business conspiracy.
explanation.walkthrough: F1 supplies FI, the numeral 1 standing in for the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: Firing someone up is stirring their enthusiasm, so firing works as an adjective meaning inspiring or encouraging.

clue.text: Nearly all ships beat a retreat

indicators.note: nearly all of a word means everything except its final letter

blocks.note: a fleet is a group of ships

explanation.surface: Almost the whole navy turning tail.
explanation.walkthrough: FLEET loses its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To flee is to run away, which is what beat a retreat means as an idiom.

clue.text: Upper missing from shoe of uncommon type

indicators.note: the upper part of a down entry is its first letter, which goes missing

blocks.note: a brogue is a sturdy shoe with decorative perforations

explanation.surface: A shoe of an unusual kind that has lost its upper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upper' is the part of a shoe above the sole, but here it is the top letter of the downward word.
explanation.definitionFit: Rogue as an adjective means aberrant or atypical, like a rogue wave unlike the rest.

clue.text: Wanting name for one to incorporate Scottish city, in brief

indicators.note: in brief means in shortened form, so the city name is cut down
to incorporate is to take into the body, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: N is the abbreviation for name
eg, for example, is often clued as for one
the Scottish capital

explanation.surface: Needing a name for someone to absorb a Scottish city, briefly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Name for one' looks like a single phrase but splits as name, then for one, the standard clue for 'for example'.
explanation.definitionFit: Wanting and needing are both participles meaning lacking or requiring something.

clue.text: Artist diving in near fish

indicators.note: diving in means plunging inside, so the artist goes into the other word

blocks.note: near is old British slang for mean with money
RA is a Royal Academician, an artist

explanation.surface: A painter diving close to a fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Near' wants to mean close by; it is the old sense of tight-fisted. RA goes in before the final Y.
explanation.definitionFit: A stingray is a flat fish with a venomous barbed tail.

clue.text: Sixteen converts taking on church life

indicators.note: to convert something is to change its form, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder
CE stands for Church of England

explanation.surface: Sixteen religious converts taking up the life of the church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Converts' looks like a noun for new believers, but it is the verb signalling a rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Existence and life are synonyms: being alive, the state of having being.

clue.text: Excellent fireplace, pushing energy forward

indicators.note: pushing a letter moves it from its place to sit within the rest of the word
forward says the letter is moved towards the front of the word, not the back

blocks.note: the grate is the metal frame holding the fire in a fireplace
E is the symbol for energy

explanation.surface: Praise for a fireplace that throws its heat forward into the room.
explanation.walkthrough: The E at the end of GRATE moves forward two places to make GREAT.
explanation.definitionFit: Great is an everyday synonym for excellent, as in a great meal.

clue.text: Popular Democrat returned in strength at the end of the day

indicators.note: returned means sent back, so the letters are read in the opposite direction
in places this pair of pieces inside the word for strength

blocks.note: something popular is in
D is the abbreviation for Democrat
might is power or strength

explanation.surface: A popular Democrat returned to office with a strong majority by close of polling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Returned' suggests re-election, but it turns the popular Democrat backwards before the pair is placed inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Midnight is twelve o'clock at night, the point where one calendar day ends.

clue.text: French are enthralled by hero's injury

indicators.note: to be enthralled by someone is to be held captive by them, so one piece is held inside the other

blocks.note: es is the French for are, as in tu es
a lion is a celebrated person, a hero

explanation.surface: French fans spellbound by a sporting hero's injury.
explanation.walkthrough: A lion is a celebrity or hero, as in lionise; French 'are' is the verb form in tu es.
explanation.definitionFit: A lesion is a region of damaged tissue, a medical word for a wound or injury.

clue.text: Roman poet's defect, ignoring primary dictatorial philosophy?

indicators.note: ignoring the primary letter means leaving out the first one

blocks.note: Martial was a Latin poet famous for his epigrams
a flaw is a defect

explanation.surface: A Roman poet's flaw was his dictatorial outlook.
explanation.walkthrough: FLAW drops its first letter to give LAW.
explanation.definitionFit: Martial law is rule by the military with normal civil rights suspended, the method of a dictatorship; the question mark marks the loose definition.

clue.text: Manuscript's opening with two historic articles? Nonsense!

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter, so only that is kept

blocks.note: the first letter of the word
ye is an old form of the, the definite article, and two of them are needed

explanation.surface: A sceptic scoffing at a manuscript claimed to be a historic article.
explanation.walkthrough: Ye, as in Ye Olde Tea Shoppe, is an archaic spelling of the.
explanation.definitionFit: My eye! is an old British exclamation of disbelief, a way of saying rubbish or nonsense.

clue.text: Novel object of obsession by detective beset by ridicule

indicators.note: something beset by another is surrounded by it on all sides

blocks.note: to mock is to ridicule
taken as written
DI is a Detective Inspector

explanation.surface: A detective's obsession that everyone else ridicules.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By' is used twice over: once as itself and once in 'beset by' as part of the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Moby-Dick is Melville's novel, and the white whale of that name is Captain Ahab's obsession within it.

clue.text: Sweet cone for us, and gala dancing

indicators.note: dancing letters move about and settle in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder
taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: An ice-cream cone for us, and dancing at the gala: a party treat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweet cone' suggests an ice cream; it is the old conical block in which refined sugar was sold.
explanation.definitionFit: Loaf sugar was refined sugar moulded into a tall cone, the form it was sold in before granulated sugar.

clue.text: Who could have no stress with vocalising, ultimately?

definitions.text: Who could have no stress with vocalising, ultimately?

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final letter of the word before it
could have suggests what the letters might become if put in another order

blocks.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A question about who finds singing relaxing.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: singers are the people who find no stress in vocalising.
explanation.definitionFit: Songsters are singers, people whose vocalising comes naturally, which the whole question describes.

clue.text: Orchestral item setter misplaced somewhere near Covent Garden?

indicators.note: letters that are misplaced are out of their proper positions and must be reordered

blocks.note: a bow is used to play the violins and cellos of an orchestra
taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A setter mislaying an orchestral item somewhere around the Royal Opera House.
explanation.walkthrough: Bow Street is a London street beside Covent Garden, long home to a famous magistrates' court and the Bow Street Runners.
explanation.definitionFit: Bow Street runs along the east side of the Royal Opera House, so it is literally a place near Covent Garden.

clue.text: Bird featured in comic story on the radio

indicators.note: words on the radio are heard rather than read, so the sound counts, not the spelling

blocks.note: a wag is a joker, and a tale is a story

explanation.surface: A bird appearing in a funny radio story.
explanation.definitionFit: The wagtail is a small songbird named for the way it constantly bobs its long tail.

clue.text: Agitated, note, very agitated

indicators.note: agitated letters are stirred up and fall into a different sequence

blocks.note: N is the abbreviation for note
taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A jittery note scribbled by someone very agitated indeed.
explanation.walkthrough: The same word does two jobs in different places: the first 'Agitated' is the definition, the second the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Nervy means jumpy or anxious, so it matches agitated as an adjective for someone on edge.

clue.text: Contemptible attention covering Scottish garment being flipped up

indicators.note: covering means wrapping around, so one word goes round the other
flipped up in a down clue means read from bottom to top

blocks.note: to have someone's ear is to have their attention
the kilt is the pleated tartan skirt of Highland dress

explanation.surface: A Scotsman's kilt flipping up and drawing contemptible attention.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'flipped up' turns the whole built word to read from bottom to top.
explanation.definitionFit: Ratlike describes someone mean and despicable, like a rat in the insulting sense.

clue.text: Baboon? Please stare

blocks.note: do as a polite request, as in do sit down
to gape is to stare open-mouthed

explanation.surface: A zoo visitor urged to stare at the baboon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Please stare' reads as an invitation, Do gape!, and those two words together are the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Dog-ape is an old name for the baboon, from its dog-like muzzle; the question mark flags it as an example.

clue.text: Slightly elevated, favouring university declaration, initially

indicators.note: initially points to the first letter of the word before it

blocks.note: pro means in favour of
U is the abbreviation for university
the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: Pleased to be backing a university's declaration.
explanation.definitionFit: Standing proud means projecting slightly above a surface, a technical sense used by builders and joiners.

clue.text: Forced voice to have no success eliminating one dispute

indicators.note: eliminating means removing, so the letter for one is dropped

blocks.note: to fail is to have no success
Roman numeral one
a set-to is a fight or argument

explanation.surface: A singer straining to win an argument and getting nowhere.
explanation.walkthrough: A set-to is British informal for a brief fight or quarrel.
explanation.definitionFit: Falsetto is the artificially high register a male singer forces his voice into above its natural range.

clue.text: Working around new edition of rag or newspaper?

indicators.note: a new edition reworks the text, so the letters are rearranged
around means surrounding, so one word goes outside the other

blocks.note: a machine that is working is on
taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Working on a new edition of a rag, a scruffy newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rag' is slang for a newspaper, which tempts one to read it as the definition, but it is the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: An organ is a publication that speaks for a party or group, like a house newspaper.

clue.text: Small book in recess

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the other

blocks.note: B is the abbreviation for book
a bay is an alcove or recess

explanation.surface: A little book tucked into an alcove.
explanation.definitionFit: Baby as an adjective means small or miniature, as in baby carrots.

clue.text: Firm importing trimmed version of fat cigar

indicators.note: something trimmed has had its end cut off, so the last letter goes
importing means bringing in, so the firm takes the other piece inside it

blocks.note: CO is short for company, a firm
lard is pig fat

explanation.surface: A company bringing in a trimmed-down fat cigar for the boss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fat cigar' looks like one phrase, but fat belongs to the wordplay and cigar alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A claro is a mild cigar with a light-coloured wrapper leaf, a term from the tobacco trade.

clue.text: Omniscient angel lies, being at fault

indicators.note: being at fault means being wrong, so the letters are in the wrong order and need fixing

blocks.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A supposedly all-knowing angel caught lying and found in the wrong.
explanation.definitionFit: All-seeing describes one who perceives everything, close in sense to omniscient, knowing all.

clue.text: Grand woman hosting leader of Lords with pleasure

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter, which is all that is kept
a host has guests inside, so the woman takes the next piece within her

blocks.note: G is short for grand, a thousand
a lady is a woman
the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A grand lady delighted to entertain the Leader of the House of Lords.
explanation.walkthrough: G for grand is short for a thousand pounds; 'Grand woman' looks like one phrase but splits.
explanation.definitionFit: Gladly is an adverb meaning willingly and happily, the same as doing something with pleasure.

clue.text: Our people back film

blocks.note: we is how people refer to their own group
the stern is the back of a ship

explanation.surface: We support our own people's film.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' looks like a verb meaning support or a reversal signal; here it is a noun, the rear of a boat.
explanation.definitionFit: A western is a film genre set on the American frontier, with cowboys and gunfights.
